catalog_quote: Stress is NOT phonemic. It occurs on the penultimate syllable of a word, except when the following suffixes are added: -ku I, me / -mu you / -na he, she, or definite / -ta we (incl) / -mo already / -pa still. In such cases the stress remains on the penultimate syllable of the word root. For example: 'sapo house, 'sapoku my house, 'ana child, 'anamu your child, 'uma father, 'umata our (incl) fathe…

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: Coding 'fixed-strict' penultimate (penultimate stress, domain word = root+suffixes, enclitics -ku -mu -na -ta -mo -pa outside the domain) rests on Barr & Barr 1988 PL A-79 p.145 §3.1, which I confirmed verbatim in the text we hold layer at the cited page; a second held Barr 1988 paper (PL A-79 p.45 n.3) independently says true suffixes (-raka, -saka) shift stress while enclitics do not, which is exactly the domain choice the record encodes. The deciding source is a dedicated phonology article by the primary fieldworkers and is the highest-ranked descriptive work Glottolog has for this languoid; no later grammar, dissertation, JIPA illustration or instrumental study was found. Only cosmetic gaps: the record's top-level quote/cite/loc/grade fields are blank (the quotation and locator live in sources/the domain quotation/the domain locator), and the quote truncates the last two of Barr's twelve examples.
